title: The invention of spinning and weaving
summary: Spinning twists fibres into continuous yarn; weaving interlaces yarn into cloth. More than a hundred perforated pebbles from the 12,000-year-old Natufian village of Nahal Ein-Gev II in Israel are interpreted as spindle whorls, flywheels for spinning fibres, among the earliest rotational tools. Woven textiles from Catalhoyuk in Anatolia, a town occupied between 7400 and 6200 BCE, are among the earliest known in the Near East and Europe; new analysis shows they were made from local oak bast rather than flax, so tree fibres mattered more than once thought.

uncertainty.note: Earliest rotary spinning apparatus attested by perforated pebble spindle whorls at Nahal Ein Gev II (c. 12,000 BP / 10,000 BCE); earliest widely documented woven bast textiles preserved at Neolithic Çatalhöyük (occupation c. 7400–6200 BCE).

importance.justification: Turned fibres into cloth, a basic technology of clothing, trade and craft in every later society (R4 D3 T4 L3).

related.because: Sewing and fitted clothing preceded woven cloth; both are textile technologies.

beats.caption: Early perforated pebble spindle whorls at Nahal Ein Gev II demonstrate rotational fiber spinning in the Natufian Levant.
Preserved oak-bast woven cloth at Çatalhöyük confirms the expansion of structured loom weaving across Neolithic Southwest Asia.
